summary: multipass is a password manager whose selling point is that it trusts almost nothing: it has no third-party crates, and its README says the only code you trust beyond the repository is the Rust toolchain. Today you install it by cloning the repository and running cargo install --path ., and there are no releases at all.

This pull request adds one file, the plan for an installer and a release process, at status: ready. Nothing is built yet. The plan has to make installing easy without adding a party you must trust blindly, so most of it is about how each download is checked.

1. An installer script. install.sh builds the tagged source with your own cargo when you have Rust. Without Rust, it downloads a universal macOS binary and installs it only after gh attestation verify shows that the repository's release workflow built it.
  2. A release workflow. Merging a version bump to main builds the binary twice to prove the build is reproducible, attests it, tags v<version>, and publishes an immutable GitHub release.
  3. A domain. getmultipass.dev, on Vercel, only redirects /install.sh to the release asset on GitHub, so you can run curl -fsSL https://getmultipass.dev/install.sh | bash.
  4. An upgrade command. multipass upgrade downloads the installer, checks its attestation when gh is installed, and runs it. multipass gains no network code of its own and never checks for updates in the background.

The first review found three problems, and this head fixes all three. The binary check now expects refs/heads/main and the commit the tag names, which is what the attestation records. Every attestation check passes the release's bundle, so none needs a gh login. The README row now says what each way to install trusts.

cards.title: Terms
cards.html:
• Attestation: a statement, signed through Sigstore by GitHub Actions, that a given workflow run on a given repository, ref, and commit produced a file with a given digest.
  • Bundle: the attestation saved as a file (.sigstore.json). With --bundle, gh checks it without a login.
  • Source ref: the Git ref the signing workflow ran on, such as refs/heads/main.
  • Receipt: the installer's record of what it installed, so status, uninstall, and upgrade touch only that file.
  • Immutable release: a GitHub setting that locks a published release's tag and assets.

cards.title: What each install path trusts
cards.html:
PathTrusts beyond the repository
Build from sourceGitHub serving the tagged source, and your own Rust toolchain
Prebuilt binaryGitHub's hosted macOS runner with its Xcode linker and lipo, the pinned rustup toolchain, and GitHub's and Sigstore's signing of the attestation
The one-linerWhoever controls getmultipass.dev, its registrar account, and its Vercel team, unless you check the script first or use the GitHub URL

groups.title: The installer and releases plan
groups.kicker: How multipass gets installed, released, upgraded, and served from its own domain
intro: The plan is the whole change. Read it in section order: § 2.1 walks through one install step by step, § 2.3 is the upgrade command, § 2.5 is the release workflow, and § 2.9 and § 2.10 cover the domain and how its website deploys. § 3 explains each choice, and § 4 lists the acceptance tests.

The checks that matter most are the attestation checks, because they are what make a downloaded binary or script trustworthy. Each one names the repository, the workflow that signed, and the branch it ran on, and the binary's check also names the commit. The release workflow runs on the merge to main and tags the commit afterwards, so the attestation records main and the commit, never the tag.

checks.text: Plan readiness: status: ready, priority: next, no owner. Every question in § 7 is decided or deferred, and the facts left unverified each carry a rollout step, so readiness does not depend on an open question.

files.note: The new plan: the installer, the release workflow, multipass upgrade, and the getmultipass.dev redirect.

checks.text: The binary check reads the commit the tag names from the commits API, which needs no login, and passes it as --source-digest beside --source-ref refs/heads/main. That is what ties the binary to the tag. When the API's limit is spent, the installer stops with status 69 and installs nothing.

upgrade downloads the bundle beside the script under its fixed name, multipass.sigstore.json, so the check needs no gh login. A release published between the two downloads makes the check fail, not pass.

The publish job holds the write, signing, and attestation permissions and never checks out the repository, so no repository code runs while it holds them. The build job, which runs the compiler, has a read-only token and refuses a run from any branch but main.
The session-unlock plan this section cites is in another open pull request. Its § 2.5 "Same binary" row does end an agent whose executable changed on disk, as this section says.
The README row now rewrites the README's trust paragraph for each way to install, and adds the one-liner only at rollout step 7, once the domain and the first release exist.
The Vercel token lives in a production environment limited to main. A pull_request run has a ref other than main, so it cannot read the token.
